study.title: Psalm 145 The eternal King, good for all and close to those who cry out
study.overview: This psalm is a continuous praise to God as the sovereign King, whose greatness surpasses human understanding, but whose government is manifested in concrete goodness: sustenance, justice, compassion, care for the slaughtered and response to those who truly invoke him. The psalmist not only describes divine attributes; he also shows the effect of this in the community: each generation passes over the works of God, the saints bless him, and all mankind is called to recognize his holy name. The psalm ends with a promise of universal and permanent worship.

outline.title: Personal Praise to the Incomprehensible King
outline.explanation: David makes a commitment to exalt the Lord continually, recognizing his greatness as something that cannot be probed or measured. The beginning of the psalm highlights God as King above all other rulers.

outline.title: The works of God are proclaimed from generation to generation
outline.explanation: The emphasis goes from individual worship to public transmission: each generation announces the works, power and goodness of God. Here appear the majesty, the mercy and the eternal kingdom of the Lord, which sustains the praise of his saints and demonstrates his royalty in history.

outline.title: The Lord sustains, answers and judges
outline.explanation: In this section, God appears as the one who raises the slaughtered, feeds all the creatures, is close to those who seek him with sincerity and protects those who love him. At the same time, he acts with justice against the wicked, leading the psalm to a conclusion of universal praise.

study.context: According to Tyndale's note, this is the last psalm of the group of Psalms of David (138-145) and begins the final sequence of psalms of praise (146-150). Adam Clarke notes that the psalm is attributed to David in Hebrew traditions and ancient versions, and also describes it as an acrostic psalm. The very structure of the text reinforces the intention to form a comprehensive confession: God is praised by who he is, for what he does, and by the way he governs and sustains his creatures.
study.theology: The psalm unites transcendence and proximity. God is incomprehensible in greatness, but accessible in mercy. His kingdom is eternal, but his dominion is not abstract: he holds those who fall, feed the living, responds to the sincere cry and saves those who fear him. Theologically, the text presents divine sovereignty not as cold power, but as holy and kind royalty. There is also a clear moral contrast: the Lord protects those who love him and judges the wicked. Praise, therefore, is not just devotional emotion; it is the proper response to the reality of God's character and government. In Protestant evangelical reading, this praise finds its peak in the confidence that the King God takes care of his people and calls every creature to recognize his holy name.

scholarViews.insight: The psalm celebrates the Lord as King of all, and highlights that his actions reveal his royal character; he also emphasizes that each generation continues to witness his works.
The psalm shows that prayer must lead to praise: whoever seeks God and receives help from him should not be limited to asking, but to thank with abundance.
The final verse calls all mankind to bless the holy name of God, because it is good for everyone, sustains life and is also a savior to those on the verge of ruin.

questions: If God is too great to be fully investigated, how should this shape my humility in speaking of him?
How are my life and my community moving forward, to the next generation, the works and goodness of God?
Have I sought the Lord sincerely, or only in times of need?
study.practice: Take a break the time to turn this psalm into personal prayer. Begin praising God for whom he is, then remember three concrete acts of his care in his life. Then practice the transmission of praise: tell the other person, in simple words, a work of God that you have seen. Finally, pray for those who are slaughtered or needy, asking the Lord to sustain them as the psalm says he does.
study.uncertainty: There is a textual observation in Adam Clarke's notes of the possible absence of a verse between the present verses 13 and 14 in the traditional Hebrew text; as this request is based on the given text, it is not possible to confirm this question from this material. In addition, the scores of commentators are interpretations and, in some points, emphasize different applications; this study presented them as interpretive voices, not as indisputable conclusions.
